issues.title: Large scale blocking of TLS-based censorship circumvention tools in China
issues.body:
Starting from October 3, 2022 (Beijing Time), more than 100 users reported that at least one of their TLS-based censorship circumvention servers had been blocked. The TLS-based circumvention protocols that are reportedly blocked include [trojan](https://github.com/trojan-gfw/trojan), [Xray](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core), [V2Ray TLS+Websocket](https://www.v2fly.org/config/transport/websocket.html), [VLESS](https://www.v2fly.org/config/protocols/vless.html), and [gRPC](https://www.v2fly.org/config/transport/grpc.html). We have not received any report of the blocking of [naiveproxy](https://github.com/klzgrad/naiveproxy) though.

Below are a summary of this blocking event and our conjuncture.

The blocking is done by blocking the specific port that the circumvention services listen on. When the user [change the blocked port](https://gfw.report/blog/ss_tutorial/en/#mitigate-port-blocking-by-having-backup-ports) to a non-blocked port and keep using the circumvention tools, the entire IP addresses may get blocked. It is worth noting that their domain names are not added to GFW's DNS or SNI blacklists.

While most of the users report their port 443 got blocked, a few users reported that their *non-443* port on which circumvention services listen got blocked as well. While most of the blocked servers are in some popular VPSes providers' datacenters (for example, the [bandwagonhost](https://bandwagonhost.com/)), at least one user reported the blocking of a server in residential network in Europe.

In a few cases (not all cases), the blocking seems to be dynamic because the web browser could still access their circumvention ports but not the circumvention tools did not work.

All these observations above strongly indicate that the GFW can indeed accurately identify and block the circumvention services, rather than simply block the port 443, or block the popular VPS providers.

Based on the information collected above, we suspect, without empirical measurement yet, that the blocking is possibly related to the [TLS fingerprints](https://tlsfingerprint.io/) of those circumvention tools. Perhaps developers want to look into [uTLS](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls). One may also find this [paper reading group](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/54), [this summary](https://gfw.report/blog/v2ray_weaknesses/en/#unique-tls-clienthello-fingerprints), and [this post](https://zhufan.net/2022/06/18/tls%E6%8F%A1%E6%89%8B%E6%8C%87%E7%BA%B9%E6%A3%80%E6%B5%8B%E6%81%B6%E6%84%8F%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6%E6%B5%81%E9%87%8F/) on TLS fingerprint helpful.

We will investigate if the GFW indeed uses the TLS fingerprints sent by these clients to identify circumvention protocols. At the same time, if you have any server being blocked, or if you have any evidence that can corroborate or falsify our hypothesis, we courage you to share your comments publicly or privately. Our private contact information can be found at the footer of [GFW Report](https://gfw.report).

We confirm that the Great Firewall of China has blocked `google.com` and all its subdomains `*.google.com`, affecting more than [1,100 domains](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/files/9690188/affected_google_domains.txt) and a large number of popular services. In this post, we introduce the two major censorship actions we observed. We share instructions on detecting common website censorship in China, encouraging more people to detect and expose censorship independently.

The censors first started **SNI-based** censorship on `google.com` and `*.google.com` on `Thursday, September 22, 2022`, sometime between between `6:23 AM` and `7:33 PM` Beijing Time (UTC+8). Specifically, the censor looks for SNI values in TLS ClientHello messages, and when a SNI value matches the blacklist rules, the censor sends forged TCP RST packets to tear down the connections.

Eight days later, the censors started **DNS-based** censorship on `google.com` and `*.google.com` on `Friday, September 30, 2022`, sometime between between `1:56 PM` and `2:35 PM` Beijing Time (UTC+8). That is, the censor check the query name in DNS queries against the blacklist rules and injects forged DNS responses containing wrong IP addresses.

Below are a list of frequently asked questions:

## Q: What domains are censored?

Any domain matches `google.com` or `*.google.com` are censored. For example, `translate.google.com` has been censored.

We also confirm that `*google.com` and `google.com.*` are **not** part of the blacklist rules. For example, `madgoogle.com` and `translate.google.com.co` are not censored in China.

## Q: What is the impact of this blocking?

More than [1,100 domains](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/files/9690188/affected_google_domains.txt) are censored, including a large number of popular services, for example: `firebase.google.com`, `translate.google.com`, `maps.google.com`, `scholar.google.com`, `feedburner.google.com`, and `ads.google.com`.

We attached [a list of affected domains](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/files/9690188/affected_google_domains.txt) to this post.

## Q: Did you observe any whitelisting rules?

No. All 1,147 `*.google.com` domains we tested were blocked without exception.

## Q: What else have you observed about the blocking?

* The start of SNI-based and DNS-based blocking both happened durin the business hours in China.
* `google.com` is censored by all three DNS injectors; `*.google.com` is censored by DNS Injector 2 and 3, but not Injector 1. (See Table 3 in [this paper](https://censorbib.nymity.ch/pdf/Anonymous2020a.pdf#page=4) for each Injector's fingerprint.)

We release this modified Shadowsocks tool today for three reasons:

原文：https://t.me/projectXtls/91

## 警惕 SNI 白名单地区隐蔽的大规模“降级攻击”

根据长期的观察，以及多位身处 SNI 白名单地区的群友的反馈，这些地区的 IPv4 TCP 并不封锁 SS、VMess 这类全随机数裸协议，与其它地区的封锁策略形成了鲜明的反差，是一种非常反常的现象。

我们已知对于封锁翻墙流量，SNI 白名单是一种附带伤害极高的方式，我们也知道，其它地区的 GFW 正在轻易识别并封锁全随机数裸协议。那么请大家思考：**为什么某些地区并不在乎附带伤害，对 TLS 采用 SNI 白名单这样的强过滤策略，却“完全不管”全随机数裸协议？**

**只有一种可能：故意留的口子，除此之外没有任何其它合理解释。** 我们已知相较于 TLS，全随机数裸协议相当于是把翻墙写在了脸上，更便于识别、掌握情况。且它们普遍缺乏 TLS 的“前向安全”等高级安全特性，非常原始，通过某种方式拿到密码就可以解密以前、以后的所有流量，非常利于监控。**所以我认为，这种 SNI 白名单+不封锁全随机数裸协议的组合策略，实质上是在迫使人们从较为安全的 TLS 协议迁移到不够安全的全随机数裸协议，是一场隐蔽的大规模“降级攻击”。**

SNI 白名单地区存在的这种非常反常的现象也从侧面证实了，**我在多个场合曾提醒过的关于全随机数裸协议的种种风险切实存在，就连 GFW 也明确希望你们使用全随机数裸协议而不是 TLS。** 目前，这些地区仍可直接使用 REALITY，且它解决了 TLS 令人诟病的 CA 风险。或者，配置 REALITY over SS：https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/discussions/1811#discussioncomment-5355075

issues.title: Popular proxy software Xray-core covered up a certification verification bypass vulnerability for half a year
issues.body:
Disclaimer: I am the reporter of the vulnerability.

Xray-core maintainers look down on "skip certificate verification" feature (i.e. the `allowInsecure` option in Xray-core) or similar options in proxy software, arguing that this is equivalent to having no security measures at all and leaves users "streaking", exposing them to the risk of man-in-the-middle attacks. However, if a vulnerability in Xray-core itself causes users to be "streaking" and fall victim to man-in-the-middle attacks, Xray-core will cover it up and act as if nothing has happened.

On [October 21, 2021](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/acb81ebe3de44e7ca197bf079f1d1122ff49b490), the `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` option, with no known issues, was added to Xray-core. This provides a double layer of security: if this option is enabled, custom certificate chain pinning logic will be performed in addition to the regular certificate verification. This also facilitates the use of self-signed certificates: to use a self-signed certificate securely, a user can enable both `allowInsecure` and `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` to skip the regular certificate verification and perform only the custom certificate chain pinning logic.

However, Xray-core later claimed that `allowInsecure` is insecure and enabling `allowInsecure` is like "streaking" and would leave users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

On [January 9, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/0ca13452b8e99824e08c2c860dd0f84a4ae2859d), Xray-core removed `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` and replaced it with a new option, `pinnedPeerCertSha256`, to stop users from skipping certificate verification (or so-called "streaking"). For self-signed certificates, both `allowInsecure` and `pinnedPeerCertSha256` must be enabled, which skips the regular certificate verification and only performs the custom certificate pinning logic. This should have helped the users to use self-signed certificates securely. However, `pinnedPeerCertSha256` contains a certificate verification bypass vulnerability.

On [January 13, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/releases/tag/v26.1.13), Xray-core released the first version containing this certificate verification bypass vulnerability. Since the old option had been removed, users had no choice but to migrate to the new vulnerable option. At this point, the certificate verification defense was already teetering on the brink of collapse. Fortunately, as long as users neither use a self-signed certificate nor enable `allowInsecure`, the regular certificate verification could still provide some protection.

On [January 16, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/760223ad70f822fcb859a217e60e038a970610f9), Xray-core modified the logic of `pinnedPeerCertSha256`, making it always skip the regular certificate verification and only performs the custom certificate pinning logic. This means a protection layer has been missing: the regular certificate verification is always skipped. If a verification bypass vulnerability exists in `pinnedPeerCertSha256` (and unfortunately, it does), the custom certificate pinning logic will fail to function, effectively leaving no certificate verification in place, which allows a man-in-the-middle attack to be successfully performed. At this point, the certificate verification defense has completely collapsed.

On February 6, 2026, I found the above certificate verification bypass vulnerability in Xray-core’s `pinnedPeerCertSha256` and privately reported to Xray-core maintainers. A man-in-the-middle attacker could insert a leaf certificate at any place in the certificate chain, and the custom certificate pinning logic would verify the leaf certificate successfully, thereby leading to the success of man-in-the-middle attacks. This is an overly simple vulnerability; even without advanced security knowledge, I was able to discover it at a glance.

issues.title: [Iran] Since Oct 2026: only ICMP echo passes Iran→abroad on some routes; ~50k pps cap, volume-triggered reroute, one-way ping blocks
issues.body:
Measurements from several Iran ⇄ Europe server pairs (datacenter, 2 vCPU each), October 2026.

## What gets through

Since early October 2026, on the routes we use, TCP, UDP, GRE, IPIP, SCTP and ESP from Iran to abroad are cut after a few packets. Only ICMP passes reliably. Base RTT is about 40 ms, and random loss is 0.2–2 %, with no relation to load.

## Packet size

- At first, ICMP echo payloads above about 640 bytes were dropped.
- Since at least 2026-10-12, full 1500-byte ICMP packets pass again in both directions with DF set: 0–0.5 % loss from 640 to 1472 bytes, no fragmentation.
- Some hosts still have a route `mtu lock 680`, so check `ip route get <peer>` first.

## Packet-rate cap

- Kharej → Iran delivers at most about 50–55k ICMP packets/s, shared by every ICMP type. That is about 33 MB/s at a 640 B payload.
- Past about 45k pps a queue builds (p99 one-way delay +300 ms) and loss rises.
- With 1400 B payloads the same path gave 27.5 MB/s down and 26 MB/s up, with 0.3–0.8 % retransmission (3–5 % at 640 B). The per-packet limit appears to bind, not bytes.

## Volume-triggered reroute

- Twice on 2026-10-12, total ICMP held above ~30 MB/s for a few seconds (34.5 and 41.5 MB/s).
- 5–30 s later, the traffic was rerouted inside Iran (base RTT 40 → 76 ms) for several minutes.
- On the new route, bulk transfers collapse to about 2 MB/s with 50–90 % loss, while light traffic is fine.
- Runs at or below ~27 MB/s never triggered it.
- This looks like a volume-based reaction, not a protocol classifier. Has anyone seen the same on other ASes?

## One-way ICMP blocks

- On some Iran IPs, echo requests from Iran to abroad are dropped (100 % loss), while pings from abroad to the same Iran IP work.
- The block comes and goes from day to day.
- Swapping direction works around it: Kharej sends the requests and Iran answers. Linux on the Iran side then also answers every request itself, so `OutEchoReps` = 2 × `InEchos` in `/proc/net/snmp` unless `icmp_ratemask` or `icmp_echo_ignore_all` is changed.
- Non-echo ICMP types (timestamp 13/14, info 15/16, mask 17/18) pass on the routes we tried.

## CDN

- Iran → Cloudflare → Kharej over `wss`: every variant without ECH failed to connect. The block comes right after the TLS handshake, which points to SNI filtering.
- With ECH it works: 44–48 MB/s down and up to 82 MB/s up with 4 sessions, RTT 109–116 ms (CDN base 86 ms).

## Tooling

The measurements were taken with WatTunnel, an open-source (MIT) tunnel I maintain. Full tables and method are here: https://github.com/JohnWatsoon/WatTunnel/blob/main/docs/TECHNICAL.md#icmp-path-limits-and-pacing

Questions I'd like other data on:
1. Is the ~30 MB/s reroute threshold per destination IP, per source AS, or global?
2. Has anyone else seen the 640 B limit lifted on other routes?

issues.title: Link-password authentication bypass through unvalidated Ed25519 identity keys, also affecting Ironwood routing authentication
issues.body:
This report is generated by AI, I am submitting in a hurry to let you know what is going on.


## Summary

We identified this during an AI-assisted source audit.

A remote peer that can reach a password-protected Yggdrasil listener can supply an Ed25519 public key representing the curve's identity point. The handshake relies on a signature under that peer-supplied key to establish knowledge of the link password. For this degenerate key, signature verification can succeed independently of the signed message, so the password-dependent digest does not provide the intended authentication boundary.

Ironwood also accepts this identity in its routing signature checks. This means its subsequent checks do not compensate for the link-handshake weakness.

This report is based on upstream source inspection. We did not execute a PoC, reproduce an exploit, or validate a live deployment. The supported conclusion is an authentication flaw permitting unauthorized peering and routing-state admission under the conditions below; arbitrary traffic hijacking is not established.

## Source examined

- Yggdrasil `v0.5.14`: [`src/core/version.go`](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/v0.5.14/src/core/version.go#L91), containing the affected link-password verifier.
- Yggdrasil `develop`, inspected on 2026-10-17: the same [handshake logic](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/src/core/version.go#L91), and [connection authorization and handoff](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/src/core/link.go#L589).
- Ironwood `4dfb1af8c1ed`, the dependency selected by the inspected [Yggdrasil develop manifest](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/go.mod): routing behavior described below.
- Go `1.26.0`: the inspected [Ed25519 public-key parsing and verification implementation](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.0/src/crypto/internal/fips140/ed25519/ed25519.go#L128), corresponding to the Go baseline declared by that develop manifest.

The release observation concerns the handshake source; the detailed Ironwood trace concerns the pinned develop dependency. We have not established the first affected release, a complete affected-version range, or a fixed release.

## Why the password check fails

issues.body:
`yggdrasilctl` exits with status **0** after recovering a panic and printing `Fatal error`. This makes shell scripts and monitoring treat a failed admin command as successful.

I reproduced this on `develop` at `6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c` with Go 1.26.9 on Windows/amd64. The same recovery path handles connection failures, invalid JSON and errors decoding typed responses.

### Minimal reproduction

Build the unmodified console:

```sh
go build -o yggdrasilctl ./cmd/yggdrasilctl
```

Run it against an invalid local TCP destination; no daemon is needed:

```sh
./yggdrasilctl -endpoint=tcp://127.0.0.1:0 getSelf
echo $?
```

PowerShell equivalent:

```powershell
.\yggdrasilctl.exe -endpoint=tcp://127.0.0.1:0 getSelf
$LASTEXITCODE
```

**Actual:** a `Fatal error: dial tcp ...` message, followed by exit status `0`.
**Expected:** a nonzero exit status, consistent with other admin command errors.
The exact dial error wording is platform-dependent.

### Cause and minimal proposed change

In [cmd/yggdrasilctl/main.go](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/cmd/yggdrasilctl/main.go#L33-L50), the deferred recovery function returns `1`, but that return value is discarded. After recovery, `run()` returns its zero result and `main()` passes it to `os.Exit`.

A named result lets the deferred function set the actual exit status while retaining deferred cleanup:

```diff
-func run() int {
+func run() (exitCode int) {
 	logbuffer := &bytes.Buffer{}
 	logger := log.New(logbuffer, "", log.Flags())
 
-	defer func() int {
+	defer func() {
 		if r := recover(); r != nil {
 			logger.Println("Fatal error:", r)
 			fmt.Print(logbuffer)
-			return 1
+			exitCode = 1
 		}
-		return 0
 	}()
```

### Local validation of the proposed change

I added subprocess regression tests that invoke the real `main()` and inspect the OS exit status. Before the change, connection failure, invalid JSON, and a malformed typed response all incorrectly returned `0`. After the change, all three return `1`.

Five additional cases verify unchanged behavior: API errors with and without an error message return `1`; a successful JSON response, version output and usage output return `0`.

- Windows/amd64: all eight cases pass; console build and `go vet ./cmd/yggdrasilctl` pass. A separate run of the built executable confirms failure status `1` and version status `0`.
- Linux/amd64 (Alpine 3.24.2, Go 1.26.9, GCC 15.2.0): `go test -json -count=1 -timeout=180s -parallel=2 ./...` and `go test -race -json -count=1 -timeout=300s -parallel=2 ./...` pass with `GOMAXPROCS=2` and `GOFLAGS=-p=1`. Each run records 67 passing test/subtest events, zero skips/failures and no race reports.
- Linux tests ran in an isolated network namespace with loopback only. This is local validation, not an upstream CI run or a live mesh test; native Windows race and other OS integration checks were not run.

I searched open and closed issues/PRs for `yggdrasilctl`, exit status/code, `Fatal error` and recovery. I did not find a matching report. Historical #641 introduced the `run()`/`os.Exit` structure but does not resolve this recovery result. This is separate from the admin daemon crash reported in #1387.

issues.title: Admin API: explicit null arguments can terminate the daemon
issues.body:
An admin request with explicit `"arguments": null` can terminate the daemon with a nil-pointer panic. I reproduced this against `develop` at `6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c` and verified a small local fix.

### Reproduction

Start a disposable daemon built from that revision with `-useconf`, supplying this configuration on stdin:

```json
{
  "AdminListen": "tcp://127.0.0.1:19001",
  "IfName": "none",
  "MulticastInterfaces": [],
  "Peers": [],
  "Listen": []
}
```

Once the admin endpoint is listening, send:

```python
import socket

with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 19001), timeout=2) as client:
    client.sendall(b'{"request":"getPeers","arguments":null}\n')
    print(client.recv(4096))
```

**Actual:** the connection closes and the daemon terminates with a nil-pointer panic (exit code 2 in my Windows reproduction).

**Expected:** an invalid admin request should receive a JSON error response without terminating the daemon. A connection using `keepalive` should remain usable for a subsequent valid request.

I also reproduced the same null-pointer failure for `addPeer` and `removePeer` in local handler tests. This requires access to the admin endpoint; I have not established reachability through ordinary overlay peer traffic.

### Cause and proposed fix

The handlers allocate a request pointer and then call `json.Unmarshal(in, &req)`. JSON `null` sets that pointer to nil, after which handlers such as `getPeersHandler` dereference it. The default `{}` assigned in `handleRequest` only covers omitted arguments, not an explicit null value.

Relevant source: [admin request decoding and dispatch](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/src/admin/admin.go), [getPeers handler](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/src/admin/getpeers.go).

My local fix adds the `bytes` import and rejects explicit null immediately before calling `handler.handler(req.Arguments)` in `handleRequest`:

```go
// Null would clear the request pointers allocated by handlers.
if bytes.Equal(bytes.TrimSpace(req.Arguments), []byte("null")) {
    return errors.New("arguments must not be null")
}
```

Omitted arguments retain the existing `{}` default. Ordinary object arguments remain unchanged.

### Local verification

- Regression tests fail for null arguments on the original code and pass with the guard. They cover omitted arguments, empty/nonempty objects, null with whitespace, rejection before dispatch, and `getPeers`/`addPeer`/`removePeer` followed by a valid request on the same keepalive connection.
- With the fix, a real Windows daemon returned errors for all three null commands, stayed alive, and accepted subsequent valid commands on the same connection. TUN, discovery and peers were disabled for this reproduction.
- Go 1.26.9, Windows amd64: build, `go vet ./...`, and the selected test suite passed.
- Go 1.26.9, Linux amd64 (Alpine 3.24.2 under WSL2, GCC 15.2.0, CGO enabled): the full suite and full race suite passed, each with 67 tests/subtests and no test skips or race reports. Commands were `go test -count=1 -timeout=180s -parallel=2 ./...` and `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=300s -parallel=2 ./...`, with `GOFLAGS=-p=1`. These ran in a network namespace with loopback only and no external route.

These are local results, not GitHub CI results or a claim of validation on every supported platform. I searched existing issues/PRs and checked the relevant changes in #1364 and #1365; I did not find a matching null-argument fix.

issues.title: core: bound ws/wss/socks handshakes with a dial timeout
issues.body:
## Summary

Only the plain TCP dial is bounded (5 s). After the TCP connection succeeds:

- the WebSocket HTTP upgrade has **no deadline**;
- the WSS TLS handshake has **no deadline** (the default `TLSHandshakeTimeout` of 10 s does not apply because the transport is built by hand);
- the SOCKS negotiation has **no deadline**.

A peer — or a middlebox — that accepts the TCP connection but never completes the handshake therefore holds the dial open until the peer is removed entirely, wasting the whole backoff cycle on a dead attempt.

## Fix

Introduce a shared `wsDialTimeout` (15 s, a variable so tests can shorten it) and apply it to each stage:

- `http.Client.Timeout` for the ws/wss upgrade (the websocket library turns it into a deadline for the handshake only, so the upgraded connection is not affected);
- `TLSHandshakeTimeout` for the WSS TLS handshake, which also bounds a dial the transport may finish in the background after the request is cancelled;
- a context-bounded SOCKS negotiation via `DialContext` when the proxy supports it (the `x/net` SOCKS5 dialer does).

Files: `src/core/link_ws.go`, `src/core/link_wss.go`, `src/core/link_socks.go`.

## Tests

- `TestWSDialTimeout`, `TestWSSDialTimeout`, `TestSOCKSDialTimeout`: a server accepts TCP and never answers; each dial must be abandoned at the timeout (1 s in the tests). Without the change all three fail.
- `TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn`: an upgraded ws/wss connection keeps working after the timeout has passed.
- The shared test logger now sets its call depth up front: `gologme/log` sets it lazily on first output, which the race detector flags when several goroutines log for the first time at once.

`go test ./...` passes, and the new tests pass under `-race`.

Closing the per-dial transport, so that cancelled dials do not leave sockets behind, is a separate follow-up: #1383.

issues.title: core: close the per-dial transport of ws/wss dials
issues.body:
## Summary

When a ws/wss dial is cancelled or times out, `net/http` may keep finishing the dial in the background and park the connection in the transport's idle pool. Each dial creates its own `http.Transport` and drops it afterwards, so these sockets stay open after the dial has returned: a cancelled WS dial left its socket open for more than 10 s in testing, and a WSS dial keeps it until the TLS handshake timeout.

## Fix

Defer `CloseIdleConnections()` on the per-dial transport in `src/core/link_ws.go` and `src/core/link_wss.go`. It closes idle connections and cancels dials still in progress. The upgraded connection is not in the pool and is not affected (`TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn` from #1381 keeps passing).

## Test

`TestDialCancelClosesSocket` cancels ws, wss and socks dials stuck in the handshake and requires each to return and close its socket within a second:

- without the change: ws and wss fail (socket left open), socks passes;
- with the change: all pass.

`go test ./...` passes; the dial tests also pass under `-race`.

This builds on #1381 and includes its commit until that is merged; only the last commit is new.

comments.body:
Thanks for taking a close look at this. I think there is one key point to clear up: the forged signature does not need to match the verifier's challenge at all, so the fact that x is never transmitted and differs between the two ends is not a barrier here.

The verification equation is:

    [S]*B == R + [k]*A        where k = SHA512(R || A || x) mod L

and x is the keyed BLAKE2b hash you described. The attack sets the declared public key A to the ed25519 identity element O. Since O is the identity element, [k]*A = [k]*O = O for every k, so the equation collapses to:

    [S]*B == R

which no longer depends on k, and therefore not on x, and not on the OOB secret. With S = 0 and R = O it holds trivially.

So the attacker never constructs a signature over x and never needs to know the OOB secret. The verifier computes its own x, and the constant signature (R = O, S = 0) is valid for whatever x it computed. Your description ("the value being verified is dynamically computed by both ends and never transmitted") is accurate, and it is exactly why this works: the message dependence is multiplied away by A = O.

On the SHA512 point: pre-hashing the message makes k unpredictable, but k is multiplied by A. No amount of hashing strength helps when the factor is a small-order point. The small-order problem is not about the message or the pre-hash; it is about A and R being attacker supplied values that are decoded as points without a small-order check. In this handshake, A is literal attacker input (m.publicKey) used as a bare point.

This is easy to demonstrate with only Go's crypto/ed25519 and no network. With A = 0x01 || 0*31 and the single signature R = 0x01 || 0*31, S = 0, Verify returns true for every message we try, including thousands of random messages and thousands of messages of the form SHA512(random password), and for messages of the exact form used by the peering handshake, keyed BLAKE2b(password, A). A random, valid public key never verifies with this signature.

Concretely, using the same construction as the link handshake, ed25519.Verify(A = 0x01 || 0*31, BLAKE2b512(key = password, msg = A), sig = (R = 0x01 || 0*31, S = 0)) gives:

    password=""           verify=true
    password="wrong"       verify=true
    password="any-guess"   verify=true
    control (real key)     verify=false

Note that x here is computed by the verifier from its own password, exactly as you described, and the constant signature still passes. The password never needs to be known. That is the whole point: the message dependence is erased by A = O.

It is also worth stressing that this is not a subtle or hard to reach condition. In this protocol the client controls its ed25519 identity and the password at the same time, and it chooses its own identity. So a client can simply pick a weak (small-order) identity and pair it with the constant signature, and the check passes regardless of the password. The natural fix is therefore to reject weak identities, that is reject small-order public keys (and ideally small-order R and non-canonical S as well, i.e. strict verification) at every site that verifies an attacker supplied key: the link handshake, ironwood's per-message peer auth, and the encrypted/session handshake. To be clear, peigongdsd has already implemented a fix along these lines.

On whether this is a bug in crypto/ed25519: not in the sense of violating the spec. Go implements the RFC 8032 verification algorithm, which does not require rejecting small-order or identity public keys. Go's verify checks the signature length, rejects a non-canonical S, computes [S]B + [k](-A), and compares it with R, but it does not reject small-order A or R (see crypto/internal/fips140/ed25519, verifyWithDom). RFC 8032 permits a low-order A, so this is a known, spec-compliant property, and it is exactly why libraries such as ed25519-dalek offer a separate strict verification mode (verify_strict) that rejects small-order points. usage of sha512 in ed25519 in message signature is as follows:

```
setup:

B = base point
L = group order
M = message bytes
h = SHA512(seed)
p = h[32:63]
a = h[0:31]
A = a * B


signing:
LE = little endian

r = LE(SHA512(p || M)) mod L
R = r * B
k = LE(SHA512(R || A || M)) mod L
S = (r + k*a) mod L
signature = (R, S)

```
OOB_shared_secret = "my-super-secret-password-12345"

A = initiator public key point
B = recipient yggdrasil router

x = BLAKE2S_512(A, OOB_shared_secret) // digest auth, hash A using shared OOB secret

R, S = ED25519_sign(x, a)             // sign digest auth result with our private key

initiator sends (A || R || S)    // sends proof that he knows the OOB shared secret

...
recipient receives: (A || R || S)

recipiant computes x via:

x = BLAKE2S_512(A, OOB_shared_secret) // compute expected digest auth result for A

issues.title: Don't send data if remote address is not set
issues.body:
SendData takes the header protection key from m_Address->i, but an incoming session has no address until SessionConfirmed. A block from a SessionRequest payload can reach SendData before that: HandlePayload parses RelayRequest regardless of session state, and HandleRelayRequest answers through SendData when the relay tag is not found. The result is a read at a null address and the router dies.

Reachable by anyone: the token that ProcessSessionRequest requires is handed out by the receiver itself in Retry, and the static key for the handshake is published in its RouterInfo.

Reproduced on 3.0.0 (ec19bfb5) with a crafted SessionRequest whose payload is a datetime block, a RelayRequest block with an unknown relay tag and padding: the router dies both under AddressSanitizer (SEGV at 0x41) and in an ordinary build (Segmentation fault). With this change the same packets leave the router alive and log 'Address is not set' instead.

Builds with no warnings, make -C tests passes.

issues.title: SOCKS and HTTP inbounds: support dynamic user management
issues.body:
## Problem

The `socks` and `http` inbounds keep their accounts in a `map[string]string` on
the protobuf config and read it without a lock on every handshake. Neither
implements `proxy.UserManager`, so the API refuses them:

```
$ xray api adu --server=127.0.0.1:10085 ...
proxy is not a UserManager
```

The only way to add an account is to edit the config and restart xray, which
drops every live connection on the inbound. On a gateway whose clients hold
long-running TCP sessions, adding one account resets all of them.

## What this does

A new `AccountValidator` in `proxy/http` holds the same username/password pairs,
built from the config at startup and mutable afterwards. The HTTP server owns
one and exposes it through `Validator()`; the SOCKS server takes that same
instance instead of building its own, because #3682 made a single SOCKS inbound
serve both protocols, and two separate stores would diverge on the first API
call.

Both servers then implement the five `UserManager` methods, so `adu`, `rmu` and
`inbounduser` work against them.

`main/commands/all/api/inbound_user_add.go` needed one change as well:
`extractInboundUsers` switches on the inbound protocol to find the user list,
and had no case for the two protocols that keep accounts in a map rather than in
a `Users` field.

## Why a snapshot instead of an RWMutex

Handshakes read the store constantly and the API writes to it rarely, so the
validator replaces the whole map on a write. Readers load the current one with
`atomic.Pointer.Load` and no lock; a writer clones it under a mutex and swaps the
pointer. A reader holding the old map finishes against a consistent snapshot.

An `RWMutex` would be simpler, so I measured both before settling on this
(Apple M3 Max, 13 and 1000 accounts, `-benchtime=300ms`):

| lookup | ns/op |
|---|---|
| bare config map, serial (what the handshake did before) | 5.6 |
| validator, serial | 9.3 |
| validator, `RunParallel` | 0.9-1.9 |
| RWMutex, `RunParallel` | 127-137 |

The handshake path costs about 4 ns more. Under concurrency the snapshot scales
while the RWMutex does not, since every reader writes to the same lock cache
line. `validator_bench_test.go` carries the first three rows; the RWMutex row
came from a throwaway benchmark that is not part of the diff.

## Behaviour notes

- `AddUser` on a SOCKS inbound whose `auth` is not `password` is refused. Such an
  inbound never consults accounts on the SOCKS side, so the account would do
  nothing there, while the HTTP side would immediately start demanding
  credentials from clients that send none.
- Users are addressed by e-mail and fall back to the username. Accounts loaded
  from a config file have no separate e-mail, and an operator naming a user has
  the username at hand.
- `GetUser` and `RemoveUser` match case-insensitively, as the other inbounds do
  with e-mail.

## Testing

- `proxy/http/validator_test.go` and `proxy/socks/usermanager_test.go` cover add,
  remove, duplicate usernames, the empty-username case, the copy returned by
  `GetAll`, and a concurrent read/write loop for `-race`.
- `go build ./...` passes, `gofmt` is clean, and `go test ./proxy/...` passes.
- `TestTagsCache` in `app/proxyman/outbound` fails on my machine, but it fails
  the same way on a clean `main`, so it is unrelated to this change.
- Live check on a running instance: a 20 MB download through an existing account
  ran to completion (HTTP 200, 81.7 s) while three users were added and two
  removed over the API, and the process kept its pid.
- In production on eight gateways since 2026-10-19, where accounts are added and
  removed daily without a restart.

issues.title: Transport: pass UDP destinations to dialer controllers
issues.body:
Native TUN's `autoOutboundsInterface` can break UDP connections to local DNS servers and local SOCKS relays. TCP to the same services continues working. The TUN controller explicitly exempts loopback destinations, but it is given the wrong address for UDP.

`DefaultSystemDialer` opens UDP sockets with `ListenPacket`, whose `Control` address is the **local bind endpoint**, often `0.0.0.0:0`. Forwarding that argument to dialer controllers makes TUN miss its loopback exemption and bind the socket to the physical interface. TCP controllers already receive the remote endpoint. On Windows the resulting UDP send fails with:

```text
write udp [::]:<local-port>->127.0.0.1:<server-port>: wsasendto: The requested address is not valid in its context.
```

Pass the resolved `destAddr.String()` to UDP dialer controllers, consistent with the TCP path and the existing outbound socket-options call. Document that callback contract. Socket creation, explicit source binding, controller error handling and listener-controller arguments are unchanged; no configuration fields are added.

### Native reproduction

Tested on Windows 10/amd64 in Hyper-V, using Go 1.27.2 builds from unmodified v26.10.17 (`92ccc939`) and from that source with only this destination-address correction. The test core processes contain no application-specific patches.

A native TUN with an isolated `198.18.247.1/30` gateway and `autoOutboundsInterface: "Ethernet"` installs the controller without taking over default routes or system DNS. After waiting for TUN to report ready, loopback UDP echo/DNS fixtures were exercised through both SOCKS and the native TUN data path. A second unmodified core supplied the local SOCKS-chain hop.

| Configuration | Successful probes | Failed probes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unmodified core, no TUN | 11 | 0 |
| Unmodified core, TUN controller active | 4 | 13 |
| Destination correction, TUN controller active | 17 | 0 |
| Unmodified core, TUN controller active, repeated | 4 | 13 |
| Unmodified core, no TUN, final control | 11 | 0 |

Both stock TUN runs failed the same cases: UDP to `127.0.0.1`, `127.0.0.2` and `::1`; local DNS forwarding; the built-in DNS client using a local resolver; and a local SOCKS UDP hop. Failed fixtures received zero requests. Direct UDP outside the test core, TCP by literal IP, and TCP through the SOCKS chain remained healthy. Hostname-based TCP also failed when its local DNS lookup failed, explaining how this can appear to break TCP connectivity too.

This affects other inbounds in the same core because TUN registers a process-wide controller. It is not limited to packets entering the TUN adapter. A fresh build of the final PR source separately passed all 17 native probes, with graceful core shutdown and the original guest runtime, adapters and routes preserved. These are controlled functional tests, not throughput measurements or an estimate of failure frequency.

### Regression coverage and validation

- The new test fails before the fix and passes after it for IPv4/IPv6, with wildcard and explicit source addresses. It also verifies that explicit source binding is preserved. IPv6 cases skip only if the local IPv6 fixture cannot be opened.
- `go test -mod=readonly ./transport/internet -count=100 -shuffle=on -timeout=90s` passed; the SOCKS and DNS-outbound packages passed too. Freedom compiles and has no test files.
- `go vet ./transport/internet`, upstream `vformat`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Transport tests cross-compiled for Linux/amd64 and macOS/arm64; they were not executed there. The race detector and full suite were not run locally.
- The broader `app/dns` suite stops at the existing `TestTCPLocalNameServerWithIPv6Override`, which receives an empty AAAA answer from its public resolver here. The same failure was reproduced on the unmodified base.

SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE opens its relay socket with `ListenSystemPacket(..., nil)`, discarding the inbound's `streamSettings.sockopt`. For example, UDP `customSockopt` entries requesting larger Windows receive/send buffers are ignored by the association socket, even though they are present in the configuration. The mixed SOCKS/HTTP inbound uses the same SOCKS path.

issues.title: SOCKS: prevent crash on failed UDP ASSOCIATE replies
issues.body:
A SOCKS5 client resetting its TCP control connection during UDP ASSOCIATE setup can crash the entire Xray process. `handshake5` creates the UDP association before writing the success reply. If that write fails, its error path calls `TempUDPConn.Close()`, but `processTCP` only installs the idle timer after the handshake returns successfully. `Close()` dereferences the nil timer instead of releasing the sockets and returning the connection error.

This is reachable with valid network input and default timeouts. In a controlled Windows/amd64 loopback reproduction against unmodified v26.10.17 (`92ccc939`), a client completed SOCKS authentication, sent UDP ASSOCIATE, and reset the TCP connection while setup was in progress. Xray exited with code 2 after one canceled request, with this stack:

```text
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
common/signal.(*ActivityTimer).SetTimeout
proxy/socks.(*TempUDPConn).Close
proxy/socks.(*ServerSession).handshake5
app/proxyman/inbound.(*tcpWorker).callback
```

Check whether the timer exists before stopping it. Let the timeout callback close the immutable socket pair directly, since the callback can run before `CancelAfterInactivity` returns and assigns `c.Timer` (synchronously for a zero timeout). Existing socket/configuration behavior is otherwise unchanged.

The regression test completes authentication and deterministically fails the UDP reply write, exercising the actual handshake error path. It panics before the fix and returns the original write error after it. Additional cases verify both sockets are closed before timer initialization, on immediate/normal idle expiry, and on explicit close with an active timer.

Validation on Windows/amd64, Go 1.27.2:

- `go test -mod=readonly ./proxy/socks ./proxy/http ./common/signal ./app/proxyman/inbound -count=1 -timeout=180s` passed.
- The UDP-association regressions passed 100 shuffled repetitions.
- A fresh core build with the fix handled 1,000 canceled UDP setups without exiting and then completed a UDP echo roundtrip through a new association. This controlled comparison establishes the trigger and the fix; it does not estimate production failure frequency.
- `go vet ./proxy/socks ./common/signal`, upstream `vformat`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- SOCKS tests cross-compiled for Linux/amd64 and macOS/arm64. Execution on those platforms, the race detector and the full suite remain unrun locally.

issues.title: SOCKS: add opt-in UDP relay socket options
issues.body:
SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE creates a separate UDP relay socket with no socket options. Add an opt-in `streamSettings.udpSockopt` block for that socket, independently of the existing `streamSettings.sockopt`. SOCKS and mixed inbounds with `settings.udp: true` consume it; unsupported handlers return a configuration error instead of silently ignoring it.

This is an alternative to #7196 addressing the TCP/UDP configuration ambiguity raised there. Existing `sockopt` retains its current meaning for each transport, and none of its fields are inherited by the new block. Omitting `udpSockopt` (or setting it to null) preserves the existing UDP behavior. An empty object requests no overrides. This adds no buffer defaults and does not change TCP handling.

**Justification:** This came from investigating UDP loss in a Windows client embedding Xray, including its local SOCKS packet-capture relays. The relay sockets still had 64-KiB receive/send buffers even when the inbound configuration requested 256 KiB. In earlier controlled Windows/amd64 tests with eight UDP flows, 1,200-byte datagrams and a host-local echo peer, the official core lost 20.79% of roundtrips at a 300-Mbit/s offered rate; honoring the configured 256-KiB buffers on both sides reduced measured loss to zero in that fixture. The local peer separated this bottleneck from Internet/server congestion. Those measurements motivate making relay socket options available; they are not a universal throughput guarantee or congestion-control solution. The explicit block provides that capability without retroactively applying legacy TCP or unscoped options to UDP.

Example (Windows receive/send buffers):

```json
{
  "protocol": "mixed",
  "listen": "127.0.0.1",
  "port": 10808,
  "settings": { "udp": true },
  "streamSettings": {
    "sockopt": { "tcpKeepAliveIdle": 30 },
    "udpSockopt": {
      "customSockopt": [
        { "system": "windows", "network": "udp", "level": "65535", "opt": "4098", "value": "262144", "type": "int" },
        { "system": "windows", "network": "udp", "level": "65535", "opt": "4097", "value": "262144", "type": "int" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The new block accepts UDP listener settings (`mark`, `tproxy`, `v6only`, `customSockopt`), reusing the existing socket-option implementation. It rejects TCP/dialer fields, non-UDP custom network selectors, null custom entries and malformed raw option values. Custom options require an explicit numeric `level`, avoiding the existing general-purpose block's TCP-level default. Empty, `udp`, `udp4` and `udp6` network selectors are supported within this UDP-only block. Existing socket-option parsing and OS-error handling are unchanged.

Validation on Windows/amd64, Go 1.27.2:

- `go test -mod=readonly ./infra/conf ./proxy/socks ./proxy/http ./app/proxyman/inbound ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/udp -count=1 -timeout=180s` passed.
- New regressions passed 20 shuffled repetitions. Windows tests verify real TCP/UDP socket buffer sizes after IPv4/IPv6 UDP ASSOCIATE handshakes, including legacy and empty settings, with different values for each protocol/direction.
- Negative mutations dropping the UDP listener options, inheriting legacy options in the SOCKS constructor, or losing the separate options during stream conversion each failed their corresponding regression tests; restoring the code passed.
- A freshly built core passed eight loopback smoke cases: SOCKS/mixed, IPv4/IPv6, absent/explicit UDP settings, concurrent TCP/UDP echo, plus HTTP CONNECT for mixed.
- Upstream `vformat` and `git diff --check` passed. Generated bindings use upstream's protoc/protoc-gen-go versions. Linux/amd64 SOCKS tests cross-compiled; Linux/macOS execution and the full suite remain for upstream CI.

issues.title: Fix Linux FindProcess for wildcard-bound UDP sockets
issues.body:
Fixes #7192 

On Linux, `FindProcess` looked up the socket by the packet's exact source
IP and port. A UDP socket bound to a wildcard address shows up in
`/proc/net` as `0.0.0.0:<port>` or `[::]:<port>`, while its packets carry a
concrete source such as `127.0.0.1:<port>`. The exact match failed, so
process name/PID routing rules could not be applied:

    Unables to find local process name: connection for 127.0.0.1:<port> not found in /proc/net/udp

Changes:

- An exact local address match is tried first; wildcard is only considered
  if there is none.
- For UDP, fall back to a wildcard socket with the same port in the same
  address family table.
- For an IPv4 source, also check `/proc/net/udp6` for an IPv4-mapped exact
  match or a wildcard `[::]` socket. Wildcard `[::]` is used only if the
  socket belongs to the current process and `IPV6_V6ONLY` is verified to be 0
  (`/proc/net/udp6` doesn't expose this flag, so guessing could misroute).
- Candidates are reduced to owning PIDs: several sockets of one process
  (e.g. `SO_REUSEPORT`) are fine, different PIDs return an ambiguity error.
- If an IPv6 candidate's mode can't be determined and there are other
  candidates, the lookup fails instead of guessing.
- `EACCES` on other processes' `/proc/<pid>/fd` no longer aborts the scan;
  it only affects the error if no owner is found.
- No TCP wildcard fallback (a listening socket doesn't send packets).

Known limitation: wildcard dual-stack sockets of other processes aren't
matched for IPv4 packets, since `IPV6_V6ONLY` can't be read from `/proc`.

The fallback path only runs when there is no exact match.

Verified manually in an isolated network namespace with a real Xray TUN
inbound: a child process sending UDP from a `0.0.0.0`-bound socket is now
matched by a process-name routing rule (previously failed with the error
above).

issues.title: [Feature Request] XDRIVE: Add configurable object naming for storage backends
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

XDRIVE uses predictable object naming patterns containing session IDs and protocol-specific markers such as `seg` and `end`.

These patterns make XDRIVE activity easily identifiable by cloud storage providers, even when the content itself is encrypted.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add configurable object naming to `xdriveSettings`, allowing object keys to be fully obfuscated instead of exposing XDRIVE's internal naming conventions.

For example (proposed configuration):

```json
"xdriveSettings": {
  "service": "template",
  "objectNaming": {
    "mode": "opaque",
    "secret": "<shared-secret>",
    "encoding": "base64url"
  }
}
```

The naming mechanism should:

- Hide session IDs, `seg`/`end` markers, and other recognizable naming patterns.
- Generate deterministic, reversible opaque names so both endpoints can identify the same objects.
- Preserve existing naming behavior when the option is disabled.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Maintaining a custom Xray-core fork or using an external storage proxy to rewrite object keys.

### Additional context

This is especially relevant for S3-compatible storage providers using the XDRIVE `template` backend, where object keys are visible to the storage provider.

issues.title: Fix fragmented TLS sniffing and add opt-in timeout rejection
issues.body:
An IP-based SOCKS connection can be routed before its TLS ClientHello arrives. In a loopback reproduction, the same 517-byte ClientHello for `www.youtube.com` takes the domain-selected outbound when sent immediately, but takes the default IP route when sent 350 ms after SOCKS success. Once dispatched, later SNI cannot change the route. Splitting the handshake across reads or TLS records also loses the domain in the current parser.

This change:

- Reassembles ClientHello across TLS records and reports incomplete TLS as `ErrProtoNeedMoreData`. The QUIC `ReadClientHello` caller is unchanged, and forwarded bytes are preserved.
- Adds an opt-in inbound `sniffing.tlsSniffingTimeout` in milliseconds. For IP TCP/443 destinations, it waits before outbound dispatch and rejects a timeout, cancellation, incomplete EOF, exhausted prefix budget, or admission overload instead of falling back to IP routing.
- Keeps SOCKS success before waiting for application data, so clients that require SOCKS success before sending ClientHello can progress.
- Preserves existing routing rules, exclusions, complete unknown/no-SNI behavior, and usable FakeDNS mappings. It does not assign unknown domains to a proxy outbound.

Example inbound sniffing settings:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "destOverride": ["http", "tls"],
  "routeOnly": true,
  "tlsSniffingTimeout": 3000
}
```

The single deadline covers first-byte waiting and subsequent classification; fragments do not restart it. Accepted values are 1–60000 ms; zero retains the existing timeout/fallback policy. The prefix budget is 64 KiB, with 1024 pending workers per dispatcher. A pending read retains its admission slot until its owner closes the input and the read exits. JSON and protobuf configuration paths both validate the option. See `app/dispatcher/README.md` for the full behavior and limits.

Other ports, UDP, and destinations supplied as domains use ordinary sniffing. The parser fix applies even when the option is off: partial TLS now continues within the existing 200 ms budget instead of hitting the two-read early exit. Server-first protocols on an enabled IP TCP/443 connection will time out; oversized or excessively delayed ClientHellos are rejected. This does not make hidden SNI/ECH or QUIC identifiable.

Validation on Windows amd64, Go 1.27.2:

- `go test -timeout 5m ./...` passed; affected tests were rerun after the final compatibility adjustment.
- `go test -race ./app/dispatcher ./app/proxyman ./common/protocol/tls ./infra/conf` passed.
- `go test ./common/protocol/tls -run '^$' -fuzz FuzzSniffTLS -fuzztime 20s -parallel 4` passed, with approximately 2.36 million executions.
- Repository formatting check, protobuf generator-header check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Built-binary SOCKS loopback comparisons cover immediate, 350 ms and 2 s delayed ClientHellos, multiple writes/records, idle and incomplete connections, timeout rejection with no outbound accept, ordinary/no-SNI routing, other ports, domain destinations, and byte preservation. The final binary also passed a 32 KiB ClientHello case. Both dispatcher APIs have regression tests, including cancellation, data returned with EOF, prefix/admission limits, and FakeDNS compatibility.

The loopback reproduction demonstrates the routing mechanism; it does not establish the cause of an individual production incident. End-user application integration and Linux/macOS execution have not been validated locally.

issues.title: UDP inbound silently drops bursts: per-session pipe hardcoded to 16 KiB with DiscardOverflow (WireGuard over tunnel/dokodemo collapses to ~1 Mbps)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [ ] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

> Reproduced on v26.7.28. The code involved is identical in v26.9.30 and on `main` (8989adf, 2026-10-08), but I have not rerun the test on v26.9.30 itself.

### Description

Every UDP session on a port-listening UDP inbound (`tunnel` / `dokodemo-door` with `network: udp`) is given a pipe of only **16 KiB** with `DiscardOverflow()`:

```go
// app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go (udpWorker.getConnection)
pReader, pWriter := pipe.New(pipe.DiscardOverflow(), pipe.WithSizeLimit(16*1024))
```

16 KiB holds about 12 full-size WireGuard packets. Any burst bigger than that, arriving faster than the outbound drains it, is thrown away. This happens whenever the outbound stalls briefly, for example while the outer TCP connection waits one RTT for a retransmit. Nothing logs or counts the drop, and the kernel UDP counters (`UdpRcvbufErrors`) stay at 0 because the packet was already read from the socket.

The UDP hub has a second silent drop point: a 256-entry channel with a `select { default: }` drop (`transport/internet/udp/hub.go`).

The common setup this breaks is kernel WireGuard → `tunnel` UDP inbound → VLESS/REALITY. The inner TCP sees about 1% loss even when the link is idle. Loss-based congestion control (CUBIC, which is also what macOS uses) collapses at long RTTs:

| Upload, 1 TCP stream, RTT ≈ 200 ms, line ≈ 47 Mbps | Throughput |
| --- | ---: |
| Raw internet, no proxy | 48.4 Mbps |
| Same path through VLESS + REALITY (TCP via socks inbound) | 45.3 Mbps |
| WireGuard → `tunnel` UDP inbound → same VLESS + REALITY, inner CUBIC | **1.3–2.0 Mbps** |
| Same, inner sender paced (`iperf3 --fq-rate 40M`) | 34.7 Mbps |
| Same, inner BBR (ignores loss; 2976 retransmits in 15 s) | 40.5 Mbps |
| **Same, pipe raised to 1 MiB (patched build)** | **12.7 Mbps from a Wi-Fi macOS client; 0 drops** |

Locating the loss: in a 10 s test, comparing WireGuard peer counters (`wg show dump`) on both ends showed **1.36%** of bytes sent by the client never reached the server. No socket on any hop (client, relay, server) reported `RcvbufErrors`. A patched build with the pipe raised to 1 MiB eliminated the loss and its drop counter stays at 0. I have not yet captured the counter at the stock 16 KiB size; I can add that run if useful.

Things already ruled out in that setup: UDP socket buffers (`rmem_default/max` = 32 MiB), outer congestion control (BBR on every hop), MTU/PMTU (frag-needed works and MSS is clamped), CPU, routing.

### Suggested fix

Make the size configurable, and preferably raise the default. Options, in order of preference:

1. Use the existing buffer policy (`policy.levels.N.bufferSize`, `xray.ray.buffer.size`) for the UDP inbound pipe instead of a hardcoded 16 KiB, while keeping `DiscardOverflow` so a stuck outbound can't use unbounded memory.
2. Or add an env flag in the same style as `xray.ray.buffer.size` (e.g. `xray.udp.inbound.buffer.size`) and a larger default (e.g. 512 KiB, matching the default per-connection buffer on amd64).
3. Either way, count dropped packets (stats counter or a debug log) so this isn't invisible.

The patch I tested (about 30 lines: env-configurable pipe size and hub capacity, plus drop counters) is ready to send as a PR if the approach is acceptable.

Two hosts A (client) and B (server), kernel WireGuard on both, Xray between them. Add latency/loss on the path between A and B, e.g. `tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 40ms loss

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.title: XDRIVE transport: Support two-step template operations (hrefPath)
issues.body:
### Why

Some storage APIs never take or return file content in the API call itself. The Yandex Disk REST API is one:
`GET /v1/disk/resources/upload?path=…` and `GET /v1/disk/resources/download?path=…` answer with JSON
`{"href": "<presigned URL>"}`, and the content goes to or comes from that URL. Today a template op is a single
request, so the template service cannot store segments on Yandex Disk through REST. The only one-request
alternative, WebDAV, is refused on free Disk accounts ("WebDAV is not available for the free tariff.", HTTP 402,
checked 2026-10-16 on a free and on a Yandex Plus account).

### What

`opTemplate` gets two optional fields:

- `hrefPath` — a JSON path (same syntax as `tokenPath`) in the first answer that holds the URL of a second request;
- `hrefMethod` — the method of that request, `GET` by default.

With `hrefPath` set, the first request is sent without the payload, then the href is called with the payload and its
answer is what Put/Get/List/Delete see. The href is called as given — no `{…}` substitution, no auth, no template
headers — so credentials never reach the content host. A non-2xx first answer is returned unchanged, so a 404 from
`/download` still reads as a missing object. Retries and the concurrency limit apply to both requests.
Templates without `hrefPath` behave exactly as before.

### Example: Yandex Disk REST

```json
"template": {
  "flatten": true,
  "auth": {"type": "static", "header": {"Authorization": "OAuth {secret0}"}},
  "put":    {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources/upload?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}&overwrite=true",
             "hrefPath": "href", "hrefMethod": "PUT"},
  "get":    {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources/download?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}",
             "hrefPath": "href"},
  "delete": {"method": "DELETE",
             "url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}&permanently=true"},
  "list":   {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources?path=disk:/{folder}&limit=10000&fields=_embedded.items.name",
             "namesRegex": "\"name\":\"([^\"]+)\""},
  "retry":  {"status": [423, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]}
}
```

With an `app:/` path and an OAuth app limited to `cloud_api:disk.app_folder`, the shared secret can only touch the
app folder, not the whole Disk.

### Tests

- `TestTemplateTwoStep`: put/get through a fake REST-style store, 404 → `errNotFound`, no credentials sent to the href.
- `TestTemplateTwoStepTransport`: a full client/server stream over the two-step store.
- Both fail without the change; `go test ./transport/internet/xdrive/` passes.

Live (free Yandex Disk account, client and server on one macOS host, VLESS over xdrive, mux on):
first run HTTPS page 13 s cold / 11 s after reconnect, 1 MB download at ~66 KB/s, 300 KB upload at ~15 KB/s,
no errors, segments cleaned up (0 objects left). Later runs the same day were slower and flakier
(HTTPS 22–33 s, some requests timing out, 24–34 KB/s), equally with the change on 0888beb and rebased on
3834e50, so that is Yandex-side variance, not the patch. Every op checked on its own against Yandex after the
rebase: put/list/get/404/delete all fine.

Docs: `hrefPath` / `hrefMethod` would need a line in the XDRIVE template section of Xray-docs-next.

issues.title: SS2022 proxy: Fix UDP session issues after client address change; Drop oversized UDP packet
issues.body:
Three UDP fixes for the native SS2022 implementation, one commit each, each with a test that fails on main.

**1. Inbound: UDP session ends when its first source address expires**

`EnsureLink` derives the session context from the inbound conn of the address that created the session. After the client changes its source address, the UDP worker of the old address is cleaned up after ~2 min and cancels that context. This tears down the outbound flow, and the next packet creates a new session and a new outbound flow (new local port, fresh replay window). Sessions are routed by client session ID (SIP022 §3.2.4), so the session context no longer inherits the conn's cancellation; the session's own inactivity timer controls its lifetime.

Reproduced with a UDP relay that switches its upstream source port mid-session:

```
16:17:29 proxy/freedom: connection opened to udp:127.0.0.1:11003, local endpoint [::]:58428
16:20:29 app/proxyman/inbound: connection ends > EOF
16:20:30 proxy/freedom: connection opened to udp:127.0.0.1:11003, local endpoint [::]:58237
```

v26.7.28 and this PR keep a single outbound flow. Test: `TestUDPSessionSurvivesOldSourceExpiry`.

**2. Inbound: data races and duplicate acceptance when one UDP session is processed concurrently**

With two source addresses, two workers can process packets of the same session at once:

- the replay window was checked and updated in separate critical sections, so the same packet could be accepted several times;
- `clientBodyCipher` was read and written without the lock;
- `sessionItem.User` was read without the lock in the single-user and relay inbounds.

The window is now re-checked together with publishing the body cipher in one critical section after validation, and `User` is initialized under the lock. Test: `TestUDPServerConcurrentDecodeSameSession` (main: `packet 0 accepted 4 times, want 1` and DATA RACE).

**3. Outbound: an oversized UDP packet ends the whole flow**

`UDPWriter` returned `ErrPacketTooLarge` for a datagram that doesn't fit into one packet (~8.1 KB payload), which ended the flow. Now only that datagram is dropped. Test: `TestUDPWriterDropsOversizedPacket`.

`go test -race ./proxy/shadowsocks_2022/` and `go test ./testing/scenarios -run Shadowsocks2022` pass.

issues.title: HTTP outbound: Fix hang on server-first protocols
issues.body:
The HTTP outbound waits for the first client payload before it sends CONNECT. With protocols where the server talks first (FTP, SMTP, MySQL, or SSH clients that wait for the server banner, which is probably what #3459 ran into with XShell/MobaXterm) the client waits for the greeting and Xray waits for the client, so the connection hangs until one side gives up.

- Read the first payload with a 500 ms timeout, like the VLESS outbound does since #1425, so a server greeting gets through after at most 500 ms.
- After the `200`, keep tunneled bytes that `bufio` already read together with the response instead of dropping them.

v2fly has the same two changes: v2fly/v2ray-core#1517 and the `Buffered()` drain in its `connectHTTP1`.

Tests (both fail on main):
- `TestHTTPOutboundServerFirst` in `testing/scenarios`: dokodemo → HTTP outbound → HTTP inbound → a server that sends first.
- `TestHTTP1TunnelKeepsDataReadWithResponse` in `proxy/http`: the proxy writes the `200` and the greeting in one write.

Also tried with real binaries: FTP to vsftpd 3.0.5 through the HTTP outbound, via Xray's HTTP inbound, squid 6.13 and Caddy 2.11.7 forward_proxy, and from a SOCKS inbound with sniffing, times out on main and works with this change. Plain HTTP latency and throughput are unchanged.

issues.title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

If an outbound has `streamSettings.sockopt.interface` set and that interface does not exist at dial time, Xray does not fail the dial. It logs `failed to apply socket options > failed to get interface ...` at **Info** level and opens the connection without any binding, so it follows the system routing table.

`transport/internet/system_dialer.go` (v26.10.10, lines 134-139; same in v26.9.9) only logs the error returned by `applyOutboundSocketOptions` and goes on to `dialer.DialContext`. The UDP path does the same (lines 77-81). The error itself comes from `net.InterfaceByName` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`. From reading the source, Linux takes the same path (the error is logged, not returned); I tested macOS only.

Why this matters. A typical full-tunnel setup on a desktop routes everything into a TUN interface handled by Xray (default route split as 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 into the TUN), and binds outbounds with `sockopt.interface` so that their own sockets do not enter the TUN again. If the bound interface goes away, the fallback sends the outbound's sockets into the TUN, Xray routes them to the same outbound, and the connection loops.

We hit this loop in practice on macOS. A separate OpenVPN client provided a corporate network through its own utun interface, and the corporate subnet was routed to a freedom outbound so that it would follow that VPN's route. At night the OpenVPN client lost its connection and its utun interface was removed. From then on, every connection to the corporate subnet (including DNS queries to the corporate DNS server) entered the TUN, came back to the same outbound and entered the TUN again. When we looked, there were about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports were in use, and other processes on the host got `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (`Can't assign requested address`) on connect until the loop was broken by restarting Xray.

In that incident the outbound had no `sockopt.interface` at all, so the loop itself is a config problem. The obvious fix is to bind the outbound to the other VPN's interface (`"interface": "utunN"`), so that it can never fall into the TUN. That does not work because of this issue: once the interface disappears, the binding is skipped and the loop is back. The only visible sign is an Info-level log line, which is hidden at the usual `warning` level.

Expected: if the interface named in `sockopt.interface` cannot be found, the dial fails (fail closed), as a bound socket does when its interface has no route. At the very least the error should be logged as a warning. A silent fallback to the routing table defeats the purpose of binding: it can send traffic into a tunnel (loop) or past it (leak).

### Reproduction Method

No server and no TUN are needed. Run Xray with the config below (interface `utun99` does not exist) and send a request through the SOCKS inbound:

```
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://example.com/
```

Result: HTTP 200. The log shows that the interface was not found and the connection was opened anyway; its local endpoint is the address of whatever interface the routing table chose (on our machine, the address of a TUN interface that held the default route).

For comparison, with `"interface": "en0"` the same request goes out through en0 (local endpoint is en0's address) and no error is logged.

Expected result: the connection through the outbound bound

issues.title: XHTTP over HTTP/2: reducing per-stream memory
issues.body:
XHTTP over HTTP/2 uses noticeably more memory than RAW on both ends. This shows up most on memory-limited clients (#5944, #6268).

Previous discussions:

- #6268: the client allocates a per-stream upload scratch buffer of `min(peer SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, 512 KiB)` and holds it for the whole life of the stream, although a single body read in Xray never returns more than 8 KiB. With REALITY/TLS straight to an Xray server the peer advertises 1 MiB, so every idle stream on a reused xmux connection holds 512 KiB.
- golang/go#79831: proposal to lower that cap to 32 KiB in Go. Open since June with no decision.
- #6663: advertising 16 KiB from the Xray server. Not planned, because a CDN in front of the server advertises its own value.

There are two separate causes:

1. **Idle streams.** The 512 KiB scratch buffer described above.
2. **Slow readers.** Go's HTTP/2 flow-control windows are fixed: 1 MiB per stream on the server, 4 MiB on the client. When the reader is slower than the link (a video player with a full buffer, a relay whose next hop is slower, a slow upload target), the peer fills the whole window and the data sits unread in process memory. While the reader keeps up there is no difference. Kernel TCP avoids this with receive-buffer autotuning. Go's HTTP/2 has nothing like it: golang/go#63520 only proposes static window settings, and a small static window caps throughput on high-BDP paths.

### Idle streams: options until Go changes

- Patch `frameScratchBufferLen` (512 KiB → 32 KiB) in GOROOT and in vendored x/net in the release workflow. This is quick, but it only reaches official release binaries; mobile apps and distributions that build from source do not get it.
- Cap the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` at 16 KiB inside Xray before `net/http` reads it (part of the proposal below). This works for every build and behind any CDN.

### Proposal

A frame-level shim between the TLS/REALITY conn and `net/http` that manages HTTP/2 flow control on its own side of the connection. It needs no x/net fork, no toolchain patch and no config fields.

- **Frame size:** the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` is rewritten to 16 KiB in both directions. On the client this caps the scratch buffer at 16 KiB whatever the server or a CDN advertises, which addresses the concern in #6663. On the server it does the same for stock clients.
- **Windows:** each stream starts at the protocol default of 64 KiB. The window grows to twice what the reader consumed per RTT (RTT measured by PING, the same idea as gRPC-Go's BDP estimator) and shrinks by a quarter at a time once the reader stays well below it. It is bounded on both sides: never above what stock Go would grant, and never below 64 KiB or twice the current consumption per RTT.
- **Roles:** the server governs uploads and downloads; the client governs downloads only. It works with unmodified official Xray and mihomo peers. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/3 are not touched. It can be disabled with `XRAY_XHTTP_FLOW=off`.

### Measurements

Idle upload streams: 40 streams on a reused connection, heap of both ends in one process.

| server | client | heap per stream |
|---|---|---|
| stock | stock | ~555 KiB |
| stock (same as behind a CDN) | shim | ~65 KiB |
| shim | stock | ~67 KiB |

Slow readers: 100 Mbit/s, 50 ms RTT, 30 sessions, REALITY.

| scenario | stock | shim |
|---|---|---|
| client, app reads downloads slowly | 146 MB | 31–65 MB |
| server, receiver of uploads is slow | 70 MB | 20 MB |
| fast then slow stream, unread data per stream | 4.2 MB | 0.17 MB |
| latency behind a bulk transfer | ~1.1 s | ~0.1 s |

Steady-state throughput is unchanged. The cost is a slower ramp for new streams: 5-second transfers are 3% slower at 30 ms RTT, 13% at 80 ms and 30% at 150 ms.

Tested with REALITY and TLS × stream-one, stream-up and packet-up against official Xray and mihomo clients, plus model, fuzz and `-race` tests and soak runs, with no leaks, stalls or data corruption.

### Description

> 简述：v26.9.8 起使用 Go 1.27 构建，x/net http2.Transport 改为包装 net/http.Transport。当 TLS 握手被阻断而挂起时，每个会话都会新建一条 TCP 连接，XMUX 的 maxConnections 实际失效，连接数和内存随会话数线性增长。使用 `-tags http2legacy` 构建可恢复正常。与 #6644 不同，这里的额外连接与 MaxConcurrentStreams 无关。

Since v26.9.8 Xray is built with Go 1.27 (`fd2ca748`, "go.mod: Specify Go 1.27.x"); the v26.9.9 release binary reports `go1.27.1`, and the release workflow builds without extra tags. With Go 1.27, `golang.org/x/net` (v0.58.0 in v26.9.9, v0.59.0 on main) compiles `http2/transport_wrap.go`:

```go
//go:build go1.27 && !http2legacy
// Transport wrapping a net/http.Transport.
```

In this mode `http2.Transport.RoundTrip` is delegated to an internal `net/http.Transport` instead of x/net's own `clientConnPool`. The old pool deduplicated in-flight dials per address (`p.dialing[addr]`), so an XMUX client whose handshake hangs held exactly one socket and all further requests waited on it. The new path does not: while no HTTP/2 connection to the host is established yet, every waiting request dials its own TCP connection.

Normally this is invisible — the first handshake completes in one RTT and everything is multiplexed afterwards. But when handshakes hang (e.g. a middlebox blackholes the flow after the ClientHello — the TSPU scenario from #6376), **every proxied session gets its own TCP connection**. `xmux.maxConnections` still limits the number of XMUX clients (the debug log below shows two `XMUX: creating xmuxClient` lines and no removals), but not the dials underneath them.

Consequences:

- `maxConnections: 2`/`3`, introduced as the anti-TSPU default (`18e28390`, #6376), no longer keeps the client under the ~4-connection limit — it opens hundreds or thousands of connections and keeps re-triggering the ban;
- memory grows linearly with hung sessions; in a memory-limited container the process is OOM-killed, taking every other (healthy) outbound down with it.

**Affected:** v26.9.8, v26.9.9 and main (`d562d894`) — all Go 1.27 + x/net ≥ v0.58.0. v26.7.28 and earlier are built with Go 1.26 and use the legacy transport. Tested: XHTTP `stream-one` over TLS (h2). I did not test `packet-up`/`stream-up` or h3.

**Field observation.** Linux client in an LXC container with a memory limit, VLESS + XHTTP `stream-one` + TLS, `maxConnections: 2` (effective config verified with `xray run -dump`, no `extra`). During a TSPU episode against one server (pcap on the router WAN):

- up to **2348** simultaneously open client sockets to that server; bursts of 26 SYNs within 90 ms;
- 1258 of 1261 new connections: SYN/SYN-ACK OK, the ClientHello is never ACKed, retransmitted for minutes;
- the process was OOM-killed twice, 193 s apart (`Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ... (xray) ... anon-rss:218772kB`); the healthy HTTP/2 connections of the other outbounds were reset along with it.

Another outbound (different server) in the same process was unaffected — its handshakes complete, so the first HTTP/2 connection is established and everything multiplexes.

comments.issue_title: UDP inbound silently drops bursts: per-session pipe hardcoded to 16 KiB with DiscardOverflow (WireGuard over tunnel/dokodemo collapses to ~1 Mbps)
comments.body:
**Environment:** v26.10.17 (`92ccc939`), go1.27.0, built from `main`.

I measured this. `app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:289` hardcodes the per-session pipe to 16 KiB and never reads the buffer policy, so `XRAY_RAY_BUFFER_SIZE` has no effect on this path — setting it to 1 MB moves burst loss from 57.0% to 58.2%, i.e. nothing.

Honoring the policy at that one call site, with amd64's 512 KiB default and **no configuration at all**, takes burst loss from **59.2% to 3.9%** (600-packet bursts, ~110 Mbps average, dokodemo-door UDP over loopback, medians of 3-4 runs). 17 lines, one file.

Three things I'd want your call on before writing a PR:

1. A naive `pipe.OptionsFromContext` would be a regression — arm64's policy default is 4 KiB, measurably worse than today's 16 KiB, and arm/mips/mipsle return 0. It needs a floor.
2. `buffer.size=0` means unlimited, which on a remote-openable inbound is unbounded per-session buffering. It needs a ceiling.
3. `DiscardOverflow` has to stay: `handlePackets` is one goroutine shared by every session on the inbound, so backpressure there stalls all of them at once.

Separately, `transport/internet/udp/hub.go:37` caps the receive channel at 256 packets with a non-blocking send and `default: buffer.Release()` — a second silent drop point, independent of the pipe size.

Two caveats: this reproduces the drop mechanism, not the ~1 Mbps figure in the opening post; and the amd64 numbers come from substituting the amd64 per-arch constant on an arm64 host, not real amd64 hardware.

Would you take a PR for this, and if so would you prefer a floor on the policy value or a dedicated UDP inbound knob? Happy to leave it here as data if you would rather handle it directly.
