issues.title: Android: auto-reconnect when the AmneziaWG tunnel stalls after idle (connection watchdog)
issues.body:
AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.1 (AWG 3.1), Android 16, OnePlus 15.
Self-hosted AmneziaWG, mobile network (Russia), battery set
to "Unrestricted" for AmneziaVPN.

Problem
After the phone has been idle with the screen off, the tunnel
sometimes stalls: nothing works (Telegram, browser) until I
manually disconnect and reconnect in AmneziaVPN. It happens
several times a day. A manual reconnect always fixes it
immediately.

What we see on the server side
We captured traffic on our server during these episodes. While
the tunnel is stalled, no packets from the phone reach the server
at all — no handshake initiation, nothing, for 4–44 minutes.
Other devices on the same server work normally at the same time.
Typical sequence: the phone wakes up, sends a few data packets
with the old session from a new NAT port (the mobile operator
changed it during sleep), the server drops them (keys older than
180 s), and then the phone never sends a new handshake. A manual
reconnect opens a new socket, the handshake completes in ~0.1 s,
and traffic flows right away.

Feature request: connection watchdog
An option to detect a stalled tunnel and restart it automatically,
for example:
- if the latest handshake is older than ~140 s
  (REKEY_AFTER_TIME + KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT + REKEY_TIMEOUT, as in
  wireguard-tools reresolve-dns) while the app has traffic to send,
  or
- if a periodic check through the tunnel (ping/HTTP) fails
  N times in a row,
then recreate the socket and re-handshake — the same as a manual
reconnect. Configurable interval and on/off switch.

Similar features exist in other clients: WG Tunnel ("Restart
tunnel on ping failure"), mihomo-based clients (fallback groups
with health checks).

Server-side keepalive does not help here: we tried
PersistentKeepalive 25 on the server for this peer — the server
cannot reach the phone after the operator's NAT mapping changes,
only the phone can recover by sending first.

Thank you for AmneziaVPN!

On Windows 10, excluding `Weixin.exe` (WeChat for Windows) from the VPN using application-based split tunneling causes WeChat video calls to fail.

The VPN connection itself works correctly, and WeChat video calls succeed when application-based split tunneling is disabled or when `Weixin.exe` is not excluded.

Important clarification: WeChat text messaging works normally in all tested configurations (A–F). I can send and receive text messages without any issues, even when Weixin.exe is excluded from the VPN. Only voice and video calls fail to connect.

The AmneziaWG connection built into AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 fails on Windows 11 26H2.

The tunnel interface is created successfully, but the client cannot send or receive UDP packets. The service log repeatedly reports errors from `WSASendMsg` and `WSARecvMsg`:

```text
wsasendmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.

wsarecvmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.
```

As a result, the AmneziaWG handshake never completes.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0
- Windows: Windows 11 26H2
- Windows build: 26300
- Architecture: x64
- Wintun: 0.14
- Protocol: AmneziaWG
- Standalone AmneziaWG for Windows: 3.1.0

## Troubleshooting performed

I tried the following without success:

- Rebooted the laptop
- Disabled split tunneling
- Disabled Kill Switch
- Confirmed that ByeDPI and Zapret are not installed
- Confirmed that DNS settings are obtained automatically through DHCP
- Flushed and renewed the network configuration
- Checked the Winsock catalog
- Checked installed network filters
- Confirmed that AdGuard and other third-party Winsock providers are not installed

The same AmneziaWG configuration works correctly:

- On a mobile phone connected to the same Wi-Fi network
- In standalone AmneziaWG for Windows 3.1.0 on the same laptop

This confirms that the server, configuration, Wi-Fi connection, UDP connectivity, and MTU are working correctly.

## Additional observations

AmneziaVPN automatically sets the tunnel MTU to 1376. The failure occurs before the first UDP handshake packet can be sent, so changing the MTU or DNS settings does not appear relevant.

Standalone AmneziaWG 3.1.0 works correctly with exactly the same configuration on the same Windows installation.

This strongly suggests a regression or incompatibility in the AmneziaWG tunnel implementation bundled with AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 on Windows 11 26H2.

## Workaround

I currently use standalone AmneziaWG for Windows for AWG connections. AmneziaVPN can still be used for VLESS.

issues.title: [Windows][Premium] Tunnel DNS rewrites chatgpt.com / api.openai.com to a proxy that drops ~70% of TLS handshakes (Codex fails with os error 10053)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
On Amnezia Premium, the DNS inside the tunnel resolves OpenAI domains not to their real Cloudflare addresses but to a proxy IP. That proxy fails most TLS handshakes, so OpenAI Codex constantly drops with:
`stream disconnected before completion: IO error: An established connection was aborted by the software in your host machine. (os error 10053)`

Browsing other sites (google.com etc.) through the same tunnel works fine.

**Environment**
- AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0, Windows 11 (10.0.26200)
- Amnezia Premium, exit Finland (exit IP in AS9009 M247, Helsinki); same result on 3 other countries
- Protocols tested: AmneziaWG and VLESS — same result
- "Use AmneziaDNS" is OFF, custom DNS set to 1.1.1.1 / 1.0.0.1 — ignored, the tunnel interface still gets `100.64.0.1, 8.8.4.4` (see also #2655)

**What happens**
1. Inside the tunnel `chatgpt.com`, `api.openai.com`, `auth.openai.com` resolve to `57.129.144.160` (AS16276 OVH, GB), after reconnect — `216.152.150.132`.
2. The same rewritten answer comes back even when querying `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8` or `9.9.9.9` directly — plain DNS on port 53 is intercepted in the tunnel.
3. Real addresses via DoH (cloudflare-dns.com): `chatgpt.com` → `104.18.32.47, 172.64.155.209`, `api.openai.com` → `172.66.0.243, 162.159.140.245`.

**Measurements (curl, same tunnel, same moment)**
| Target | Success |
|---|---|
| `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses` via proxy IP (AmneziaWG) | 2 / 10 |
| same via proxy IP (VLESS) | 5 / 15 |
| `https://api.openai.com/v1/models` via proxy IP | 1–2 / 4–5 |
| same endpoints via real IP (`curl --resolve chatgpt.com:443:104.18.32.47`) | 15 / 15, 5 / 5 |

Failures are `curl: (35) schannel: failed to receive handshake, SSL/TLS connection failed` after ~0.4–1.5 s.
Via the real IP OpenAI answers normally (`401 Unauthorized` without a token — no region block), so the proxy is not needed for this exit.

**Workaround**
Pinning real IPs in the `hosts` file (traffic still goes through the tunnel, just bypassing the proxy) fixes Codex completely.

**Expected behavior**
- Either don't rewrite OpenAI domains for exits where OpenAI is reachable directly, or fix the proxy.
- Respect the "Use AmneziaDNS" switch / custom DNS on Premium, or clearly show in the UI that it is ignored.

Possibly related: #2655, #2375, #2996

```markdown
### Summary

We propose adding native support for
**URL-based configuration subscriptions** to
the AmneziaVPN client, following the de-facto
ecosystem standard established by clients
like Happ, Incy, v2rayN/v2rayNG, Hiddify, and
Sing-box.

Currently, configurations in AmneziaVPN must
be imported individually (one `vpn://` key,
file, or QR code at a time). For
administrators managing multiple servers or
adjusting endpoints during ongoing ISP/DPI
blocks, this creates severe manual overhead.

---

### Background & Technical Context

In the current client architecture:
1. **Self-hosted configs are completely
static:** There is no mechanism for an
administrator to push updated endpoints (IPs,
ports, or AmneziaWG obfuscation parameters
like `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`/`H1`-`H4`) to
end-users without manually issuing new keys.
2. **Legacy API v1 was deprecated:** The
historical `api_endpoint` field in JSON
configs is now rejected with
`ErrorCode::LegacyApiV1NotSupportedError` in
`importController.cpp`.
3. **Amnezia Gateway v2/v3 is proprietary &
hardcoded:** The modern auto-updating
subsystem (`SubscriptionController` +
`libagw`) relies on hardcoded keys and
endpoints (`PROD_AGW_PUBLIC_KEY`,
`PROD_S3_ENDPOINT` in `CMakeLists.txt`) and
is restricted to `amnezia-premium`,
`amnezia-free`, and `external-premium`.
Self-hosted admins and third-party community
providers cannot use it.

Introducing a standard HTTP(S) subscription
mechanism solves this cleanly without
burdening Amnezia's own gateway
infrastructure.

---

### Proposed Solution & Specifications

#### 1. Import Mechanism
* **Input:** Allow importing via HTTPS URL
(pasting URL, scanning a subscription QR
code, or opening via Deeplink).
* **Deeplink:** Support 1-click import via
custom scheme, e.g.:

`amnezia://import-sub?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexamp
le.com%2Fsub`
* **Grouping:** Imported servers should
automatically be grouped under the
subscription name in the UI.

#### 2. Subscription Payload Format
* A standard HTTP(S) `GET` endpoint returning
a list of configurations (plain text or
standard Base64-encoded, newline-separated):
  * `vpn://...` connection strings.
  * Native AmneziaWG / AmneziaXRay (VLESS)
JSON blocks or WireGuard configs.

#### 3. Standard HTTP Headers Support
Adopt standard subscription metadata headers
widely supported across clients:
* **`profile-title`** (or
`Content-Disposition: filename=...`): Display
name of the subscription / server group.
* **`profile-update-interval`**: Recommended
auto-refresh interval in hours (e.g. `12` or
`24`).
* **`subscription-userinfo`**: Key-value
pairs for quota and validity:
  `upload=1073741824; download=5368709120;
total=107374182400; expire=1735689600`
  *(Used to render remaining data transfer
and subscription expiration date in the UI).*
* **`profile-web-page-url`**: URL to user
billing/dashboard.
* **`support-url`**: URL to support
channel/bot.

#### 4. Synchronization & Update Lifecycle
* **Update triggers:**
  * Automatically on application startup.
  * Periodically in the background via a
timer derived from `profile-update-interval`.
  * On-demand via a manual "Refresh
Subscription" button in the UI.
* **Diff reconciliation:**
  * Servers removed from the subscription URL
should be deleted or marked inactive.
  * Newly added servers are registered into
the subscription group.
  * Modified endpoints (changed IP, port, or
AWG parameters) are updated in-place without
breaking client-side custom settings (like
split tunneling rules).

#### 5. User Management & Controls
* Option to rename the subscription group.
* Toggle to enable/disable background
auto-updates.
* Option to delete the entire subscription
and all associated profiles in one click.

issues.title: feat: strict split tunneling for AmneziaWG and WireGuard on Android
issues.body: Addresses #2457 for AmneziaWG and WireGuard: with per-app split tunneling, an app excluded from the VPN can bind a socket to `tun0` (`curl --interface tun0`, `SO_BINDTODEVICE`, an unprivileged ping socket) and reach the VPN server, which reveals the server's address. This adds an opt-in setting that blocks that. It is the last of three PRs, and the other two carry the datapath (merge order below). ## What the user gets A **"Strict split tunneling"** switch, shown on Android only and off by default. It sits under "App-based split tunneling" in the split tunneling drawer on the home screen and in Settings → Connection. The app split tunneling page itself is unchanged. - Description: *Blocks bypasses of the tunneling rules. Strictly prevents apps from using the VPN tunnel directly unless they are allowed to use the VPN. Supports AmneziaWG and WireGuard.* - It is enabled only when app split tunneling is on, the default server's protocol is AmneziaWG (either container) or WireGuard, and the VPN is disconnected. The setting is read when the tunnel starts, like the rest of split tunneling. - Turning it on first shows a question drawer that explains what it does and the Private DNS caveat below. | | | | | |---|---|---|---| | Off by default | Turning it on explains the trade-off | On | Locked while connected | ## How it works - `StrictSplitTunnelGuard` (`android/utils`) decides per connection. It asks `ConnectivityManager.getConnectionOwnerUid` (API 29+) for the owning app and applies include or exclude mode to the app lists. An unresolved owner is denied. Android returns `INVALID_UID` both when no socket matches and when the owner is not covered by this VPN, and an excluded app is exactly the second case. The guard keeps no state: amneziawg-go caches its verdicts per 5-tuple and asks from several threads at once. - `Wireguard.kt` registers the guard with the AmneziaWG backend through `GoBackend.awgSetUidFilter` right before the tunnel is turned on. It clears the guard on every path that turns the tunnel off. amneziawg-go drops denied packets before encryption. - The setting follows the `killSwitch` chain end to end: - a key in `configKeys`; - storage in `secureAppSettingsRepository`, included in backup and reset; - properties on `SettingsController` and `SettingsUiController`; - a flag in the VPN configuration. `ServersUiController` gains one property that tells the switch whether the default server's protocol enforces it. - Off by default, and free when off: no guard is created and the bridge is never called. ## Limitations - **Private DNS by hostname, in "only the apps from the list" mode.** The system resolver's own queries are not covered by an include-mode VPN, so the platform hides their owner, and they are denied. Listed apps then resolve nothing, and Android shows "no internet" for the VPN network. With Private DNS off or on "Automatic" everything works: in Automatic, Android falls back to plain DNS. There is no safe exception to make. Allowing the resolver's traffic to the DNS servers would also let an excluded app query `whoami.cloudflare` through `tun0`. The question drawer tells the user this. Exclude mode is not affected. - **TCP bound to `tun0` from an app inside the VPN.** With strict mode on, such a connection is denied, while the same connect without binding works, and UDP bound to `tun0` works too. `curl --interface tun0` from an allowed app i

issues.title: [Android] [Critical] Per-app split tunneling bypass for AmneziaWG 2.0 allows blacklisted apps to see the ip address of the VPN.
issues.body:
**Summary**
It was mentioned in the previous commit but the person responsible for fixing it did it only for XRay so I feel obligated to mention it again. You can get the ip of the VPN server by explicitly going through the tun0 interface. Like this (in Termux).  `curl -s https://ifconfig.me/ip --interface tun0`
That will allow any spyware (which now includes every russian big-tech app) to not only get the fact that you use a VPN but also get the ip address of the server. Then they can log it, and later block it.


**Environment**

- App version: 4.8.14.5
- Android version: 14
- Device: Samsung Galaxy A33 5G
- Protocol used: AmneziaWG 2.0
- Split tunneling: Enabled (Termux excluded from VPN)

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
 1. Install AmneziaVPN and configure a working connection.
 2. Enable Per-app VPN (split tunneling) and exclude Termux (or any test app with INTERNET permission).
 3. Connect to the VPN.
 4. In Termux, run:
```
#Send traffic through the tun0 interface
curl -s https://ifconfig.me/ip --interface tun0
# Observed: VPN exit IP`

```
**Expected behavior**
Applications excluded from VPN routing should not be able to send traffic through the VPN tunnel via a localhost proxy, unless this behavior is explicitly documented and user-controlled. If a local listener is required for internal purposes, access should be restricted to the app's own components.

**Security Impact**
If the proxy accepts unauthenticated connections and forwards traffic through the VPN tunnel:

-  User-configured per-app routing policies can be bypassed by any app with INTERNET permission.

-  Traffic that the user explicitly intended to route directly may leak through the VPN (or vice versa).

-  The presence of an open, unauthenticated localhost proxy may serve as a detectable signal of VPN usage to monitoring applications.

**Operational relevance**
In environments where applications or platforms monitor network behavior for signs of VPN usage, this issue may increase the detectability of VPN use. Because an app excluded from VPN routing can still access the VPN tunnel via localhost, it can both infer that the VPN is active and send probe traffic through the tunnel. This may also aid enumeration of VPN egress IPs and contribute to blocking of VPN endpoints. This consideration is particularly relevant given recent reports of app-level VPN detection guidelines being distributed to IT platforms [1][2].

**Suggested Mitigations**
The same that solved SOCKS5 leak (will be solved if someone merges [this](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/pull/2453) pull request).

-  Require authentication (username/password) for the tun0 interface, if the feature is intended for external use.
-  If there is any alternative way to get the VPN ip address without being in the split-tunneling whitelist - fix it.

I repeat that this vulnerability while not as critical poses a significant threat to the VPN's hosted on private servers which were mostly immune to the direct ip blocking from Russian censors.

issues.title: [Bug] AmneziaWG 2 Docker container has IPv4 forwarding disabled after automatic installation in Proxmox LXC
issues.body:
**Title: [Bug] AmneziaWG 2 Docker container has IPv4 forwarding disabled after automatic installation in Proxmox LXC**

### Environment

- Host: Proxmox VE
- Guest: Debian 13, unprivileged LXC with nesting enabled
- VPN: AmneziaWG 2, installed automatically using the official Amnezia Android app
- Docker: 26.1.5+dfsg1 (installed by Amnezia)
- Also reproduced with preinstalled Docker 29.8.0
- `/dev/net/tun` passed through from Proxmox into LXC
- Container: `amnezia-awg2`

### Problem

The official Android app successfully installs AmneziaWG 2. The client establishes a VPN connection and completes the handshake, but neither internet nor LAN traffic works.

The VPN interface, UDP listener, NAT rules, and firewall rules are present.

The underlying problem is that IPv4 forwarding is disabled **inside the AmneziaWG Docker container**, despite being enabled in the parent LXC.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a fresh Debian 13 unprivileged Proxmox LXC with Docker nesting and TUN passthrough.
2. Install AmneziaWG 2 using the official Android app, allowing it to install Docker.
3. Connect from Android.
4. Observe a successful handshake but no internet or LAN connectivity.
5. Run:

   `docker exec amnezia-awg2 sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward`

   Result: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`

6. Enable forwarding:

   `docker exec amnezia-awg2 sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`

7. Internet and LAN connectivity immediately work, without restarting the VPN.

### Investigation

- Parent LXC: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1`
- Amnezia Docker container: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`
- Container NAT and FORWARD rules are configured correctly.
- The generated `/opt/amnezia/start.sh` configures the tunnel, iptables and MASQUERADE rules but does not enable IPv4 forwarding.
- Docker inspect shows only `net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1` under `HostConfig.Sysctls`.
- A fresh Docker container also defaults to forwarding disabled.
- Reproduced with two Docker versions and a completely fresh LXC installation.
- A separate installation in a full Debian VM works without manual intervention.

### Expected behavior

The official installer should explicitly enable IPv4 forwarding inside the VPN container, regardless of the default networking behavior of Docker or the host environment.

### Suggested fix

Include `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` in the Docker container's sysctl configuration alongside `net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1`.

Alternatively, ensure forwarding is enabled during the VPN container's initialization.

This should allow the Android app to manage installation, restarts, and updates without manual intervention.

### Impact

The installer reports success, and the VPN handshake succeeds, but all routed traffic fails. This is difficult to diagnose because the Docker container appears healthy and the client appears connected.

comments.body:
## Additional Findings — Root Cause, Verified Workaround, and Recommended Fix

Further investigation identified why AmneziaWG 2 fails to route traffic when installed through the official Android app inside an unprivileged Proxmox LXC.

### Root Cause

1. The AmneziaWG 2 Dockerfile configures numerous networking parameters in `/etc/sysctl.conf`, but does not include `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`.

2. The Dockerfile initially creates a placeholder `/opt/amnezia/start.sh`, which the official Android app subsequently replaces with a generated startup script.

3. The generated startup script successfully initializes the `awg0` interface and configures iptables FORWARD and MASQUERADE rules, but never enables IPv4 forwarding.

4. Docker creates the container with only the following explicit sysctl setting:

   `net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1`

5. IPv4 forwarding is enabled in the parent LXC (`net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`), but disabled inside the AmneziaWG Docker container (`net.ipv4.ip_forward=0`).

6. The problem was reproduced on two installations:
   - Existing unprivileged Proxmox LXC with Docker 29.8.0.
   - Completely fresh Debian 13 unprivileged Proxmox LXC, allowing Amnezia to install Docker 26.1.5 itself.

A separate installation in a full Debian VM works without modification.

### Verified Workaround

Adding the following line immediately after `#!/bin/bash` in `/opt/amnezia/start.sh` resolves the routing failure:

```bash
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
```

This can be applied from the LXC using a single command:

```bash
docker exec amnezia-awg2 sh -c 'grep -q "^sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1$" /opt/amnezia/start.sh || sed -i "2i sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1" /opt/amnezia/start.sh'
```

After enabling forwarding, both internet and LAN connectivity work immediately through the VPN.

**Reboot test: PASSED.**

The modified startup script survives a normal LXC reboot and automatically enables forwarding when the AmneziaWG container starts.

No Docker image rebuild, Docker downgrade, or additional networking changes were required.

### Recommended Upstream Fix

The preferred solution is to explicitly configure IPv4 forwarding when Amnezia creates the Docker container, alongside the existing `src_valid_mark` setting:

```yaml
sysctls:

comments.body: I've put together a complete fix for this on AmneziaWG and WireGuard, measured on a device, as three PRs: - amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-go#199: a filter that drops outbound packets whose owning app the split-tunnel policy does not allow - amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-android#104: a JNI bridge, so the policy can ask `ConnectivityManager.getConnectionOwnerUid` who owns a connection - amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client#3199: an opt-in setting "Block disallowed apps from the tunnel" (off by default, Android only) and the wiring On a Poco F7 (Android 16) with an AmneziaWG server (protocol 3.1), the probes from an excluded app gave 0 of 6 with the setting on and 6 of 6 with it off. They covered `curl --interface tun0`, TCP and UDP with `SO_BINDTODEVICE`, and ICMP. Both include and exclude mode were tested. The setting, on an English build: | | | | | |---|---|---|---| | Off by default | Turning it on explains the trade-off | On | Locked while connected | Some findings may save time whoever implements this, whichever code ends up merged: 1. **Ping leaks too.** Any app can open an unprivileged ICMP ping socket, bind it to `tun0` and ping a host it controls. The owner of an ICMP packet cannot be resolved, so a filter has to drop what it cannot attribute. @makekryl's #174 (amneziawg-go) already does this, and that is how I noticed my first version let ping through. 2. **`getConnectionOwnerUid` returns `INVALID_UID` for any app not covered by your own VPN**, not only when no socket matches. That is AOSP's `ConnectivityService`. So "unresolved" is exactly the excluded app, and denying it is correct rather than a fallback. 3. **Closed sockets belong to UID 0.** After an app calls `close()`, the lookup reports UID 0. If a filter re-judges packets after its cache expires, it drops the FIN of legitimate connections in include mode. Deciding TCP on SYN only avoids that. 4. **Private DNS by hostname does not work in include mode.** The system resolver's own queries are not covered by an include-mode VPN, so they cannot be attributed, and listed apps resolve nothing. Automatic and Off work. Letting DNS through is not a safe exception: an excluded app could query `whoami.cloudflare` via `tun0`. A test build with all three parts, signed with my own key, is here if you want to check it on your own device: https://github.com/amnezia-tun0-fix/amnezia-client/releases/tag/v5.0.3.1-strict.8 — it installs next to the official app, as «strct-AmnzVPN», and from this build on tells you about newer ones; the notes there say what else to know. The notes behind all this, with the probes: https://github.com/amnezia-tun0-fix/strict-split-tunneling-notes The Xray datapath has an implementation in my forks as well: tun2socks, libxray and `Xray.kt`, linked in the client PR. issues.title: feat(tun): add an L3 TUN that carries whole IP packets
issues.body:
## Summary

Adds an optional `l3tun` mode that copies whole IP packets between a local TUN device and QUIC datagrams. It does not terminate TCP or UDP. The intended use is to run VXLAN (or any other IP protocol) between the two TUNs, so the overlay keeps a normal 1500-byte inner MTU instead of squeezing VXLAN through `udpForwarding` and a reduced MTU.

Both ends opt in. The client sends `Hysteria-L3: true` on the existing auth request only when `l3tun` is configured, and the server grants it only when it has `l3tun` as well. The header is also sent as `false` otherwise; an older peer ignores the unknown header. L3 datagrams use session id 0 and a zero address-length byte, which `ParseUDPMessage` already rejects, so an older peer drops them.

## How packets are carried

One IP packet is sent as one QUIC datagram. If that datagram is larger than the peer's current payload limit (`quic.DatagramTooLargeError`), it is split into evenly sized fragments.

The datagram prefix is 11 bytes:

```
SessionID u32 = 0 | PacketID low 16 | FragID u8 | FragCount u8 | 0x00 | PacketID high 16 | IP packet
```

Fragments of different packets may interleave and are reassembled by the 32-bit packet id. A missing fragment drops the whole packet. There is no fragment retransmission; an inner TCP retransmits. Reassembly gives up after 200 ms. The largest IP packet is 1600 bytes. A 1600-byte packet under the usual 1200-byte datagram frame is two fragments of about 800 bytes.

The server keeps one L3 peer: the latest authenticated client that requested L3 replaces the previous one. Packets read from the local TUN while no peer is connected are discarded. Before a received packet is written into the local TUN, its source address must equal the configured `peer`.

The client L3 device stays up across QUIC reconnects. Traffic is counted with the existing `TrafficLogger`, in the same direction as UDP proxying.

`l3tun` is supported on Linux, Darwin, Windows, and Android (sing-tun). Creating the device needs root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN`. Hysteria creates and addresses `hytun0` only. The operator adds the VXLAN interface after the TUN exists. VXLAN's UDP port stays inside the tunnel, so it does not need a public firewall opening.

## Configuration

Client:

```yaml
l3tun:
  name: hytun0
  mtu: 1600
  address: 10.200.0.2/30
  peer: 10.200.0.1
```

Server:

```yaml
l3tun:
  name: hytun0
  mtu: 1600
  address: 10.200.0.1/30
  peer: 10.200.0.2
```

`mtu` defaults to 1600 and cannot be higher. `address` is a prefix; `peer` must be the same IP version. A `/30` gives a connected route, so this tunnel does not need IP forwarding and does not capture the path back to the server's public address.

Operator notes, including the VXLAN commands, are in `VXLAN.md` (currently written in Chinese). For an inner MTU of 1500 the outer packet is about 1550 bytes (Ethernet 14 + VXLAN 8 + UDP 8 + IPv4 20), which fits in the 1600-byte TUN without kernel fragmentation:

```bash
ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 10.201.0.1
```

## Test results

Measured on this branch, Linux amd64 at both ends. `hytun0` MTU 1600. VXLAN between the two TUN addresses. Path: a residential PPPoE link (uplink about 40 Mbps) to a Tokyo VPS, then to a second Tokyo host running iperf3 3.16. The iperf3 client is 3.9. Brutal limits on the client were 90 Mbps up and 200 Mbps down, with loss compensation disabled. The QUIC max datagram frame size is 1200 bytes.

Same-region control, VPS to the iperf3 host, 8 seconds: 4374 Mbps up, 4441 Mbps down. The iperf3 server is not the bottleneck.

Tunnel RTT to that host, 10/10: min / avg / max 60.4 / 66.3 / 97.9 ms.
